analysis.one_liner: Taxes 100% of electricity producers' windfall profits and rebates the money to electricity consumers.
analysis.headline: Sen. Boxer's bill to tax electricity windfall profits and rebate consumers never got a committee vote; it died with zero cosponsors after referral to the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: During the California electricity crisis, Sen. Barbara Boxer proposed a 100% excise tax on windfall profits from selling electricity — profits above what state utility commissions consider a reasonable rate of return. The money would go into a federal trust fund and flow back to individual and business electricity consumers as rebates, triggered when a state's governor petitioned for them. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired at the end of the 107th Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Individual and business electricity consumers, especially in states hit by price spikes like California, would receive rebates funded by the tax on producers' excess profits [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill imposes an excise tax equal to 100% of the windfall profit — the profit from selling electricity above a 'reasonable profit' level determined by averaging state public utility commission decisions — paid by the electricity producer [S2] [S3].

Revenues go to a Consumer Utilities Turnback Trust Fund and are available, without further appropriation, for rebates to individual and business electricity consumers when a state's governor petitions for them; the bill's stated purpose is to transfer windfall profits 'to fund assistance, in the form of rebates, for individual and business consumers' [S2] [S3].

The bill cites findings that net income for electricity production for California consumers rose 333% between the second quarters of 1999 and 2000 while consumers faced approved rate hikes of 7 to 15 percent [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Electricity producers, who would owe a tax equal to their entire profit above the state-approved reasonable return; they could also be expected to argue administrative complexity and effects on investment in generation.

drawbacks.text: Defining 'reasonable profit' by averaging state public utility commission determinations nationwide would be a blunt instrument: rates and profit norms vary widely by state and market structure, so a producer in a competitive market could owe tax on profit that another state's regulator would deem ordinary — a design question an honest supporter would have to answer [S3].

A 100% tax on profits above a benchmark gives producers no upside above that line, which critics of windfall profits taxes generally argue discourages investment in new generation — a real concern during a period of climbing natural gas prices and tight electricity supply [S2] [S3].

Rebates are conditional: funds only flow to consumers in a state whose governor petitions the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, and must be spent within the fiscal year they become available, so consumers in states without an active governor would get nothing [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea is a direct transfer from producers' crisis-era excess profits back to the consumers who paid the high rates, which would have been substantial relief in states like California. The design is rough: a nationwide 'reasonable profit' benchmark is a crude way to define a windfall, and a 100% marginal tax could chill investment in new power plants at a time of tight supply. The rebates' dependence on a gubernatorial petition is a workable trigger but adds a political step between the tax and the relief.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, no cosponsor ever joined, and it expired when the 107th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Barbara Boxer introduced the bill on January 24, 2001, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance that same day [S5].
The bill attracted zero cosponsors over its entire life in Congress [S4].

The Committee on Finance never reported the bill, and no further action of any kind appears in its history after the referral — it died in committee when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Electricity producers kept their windfall profits untaxed, and consumers — including Californians facing the rate hikes the bill cited — never received the proposed rebates.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Electricity producers, who kept windfall profits

for.name: Sen. Barbara Boxer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or reported the bill; it sat after referral until the Congress expired.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee of referral, never acted on the bill during the 107th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: A single Democrat sponsored the bill and no senator of either party cosponsored it, so the bill never drew bipartisan support; the Republican-chaired Finance Committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would tax away 100% of any profit above state-approved reasonable levels, so producers' crisis-era excess earnings were directly at stake. The bill's findings tie those record profits to the higher rates ordinary consumers were paying, putting the industry's gain at odds with consumer relief [S3].

industries.industry: State public utility commissions and federal energy regulators (FERC)
industries.note: The bill gives state commissions' profit determinations a central role in defining the tax and hands FERC authority to administer the rebate fund — an expansion of regulatory responsibilities, not an industry gain or loss [S3].
